description_full: Miller Industries, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, manufactures and sells towing and recovery equipment. It provides wreckers that are used to recover and tow disabled vehicles and other equipment; and car carriers, which are specialized flat-bed vehicles with hydraulic tilt mechanisms, which are used to transport new or disabled vehicles and other equipment. The company also offers transport trailers for moving multiple vehicles for auto auctions, car dealerships, leasing companies, and other similar operations. It markets its products under the Century, Vulcan, Chevron, Holmes, Challenger, Champion, Jige, Boniface, Omars, Titan, and Eagle brand names. The company sells its products through independent distributors in North America, and Canada, Mexico; and through prime contractors to governmental entities. Miller Industries, Inc. was founded in 1990 and is headquartered in Ooltewah, Tennessee.

financial_summary: Miller Industries, Inc. is a small-cap consumer cyclical business with a $546M market cap on $790M of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -2% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, and a shrinking top line is the hardest headwind any business can overcome.

Returns on capital run at 7% against a 9% cost of capital, which means the business is destroying value with every dollar it reinvests, and 11% gross margins are typical of commodity economics where competitors can replicate the product cheaply.

The business throws off $85M in free cash flow — roughly 11 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 4.29× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.7× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 49× is fortress-like.
Shareholder yield of 2.8% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 5.3% of the shares.

sector_headwinds.text: Low reinvestment-driven growth suggests the compounding engine has stalled
Fragmented industry with below-average profit capture — no moat to protect margins
Gross margin trails most Consumer Cyclical peers — competitors appear to have the pricing hand
Consumer demand is fundamentally cyclical — a recession compresses both unit volume and pricing power, and operating leverage cuts both ways.
E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.
